summary: Describes a general syntax for data that may have cryptography applied to it, such as digital signatures and digital envelopes. It is an informational copy of an RSA Laboratories standard that later formed the basis for the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 2315 describes a format for packaging data with cryptographic information. Its six content types support plain data, signatures, encrypted envelopes, digests, and combinations of those features.

questions: what is the difference between signed data and enveloped data
subtitle: A general ASN.1 syntax for packaging data with signatures, digests, certificates, and encryption.

tldr.problem: Applications that sign or encrypt messages need a common structure for content, cryptographic results, recipients, and certificates.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #7 defines a ContentInfo wrapper and six content types that can encapsulate data with signatures, digests, or encryption information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2315 is an Informational publication of PKCS #7 version 1.5. It leaves certificate-policy choices and text encoding of binary output outside its scope.

today: RFC 2315 is an Informational RFC published in March 1998. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Scope of PKCS #7
sections.content:
PKCS #7 defines a general syntax for data to which cryptographic operations have been applied, including digital signatures and digital envelopes. Its recursive structure allows content to be nested, such as signed data inside an encrypted envelope. Attributes such as signing time may also be included and authenticated with the content.

The memo is compatible with Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM) for specified signing and signing-and-enveloping cases. It does not choose which certificate authorities to trust or define their policies. Its encoded values are intended to be BER-encoded octet strings, but it does not specify how to convert those strings for mail systems that cannot reliably transmit arbitrary binary data.
sections.plainLanguage: The format describes how to package data with cryptographic operations and related information. It does not decide which certificate issuers a user should trust.

sections.title: ContentInfo and the Content Types
sections.content:
The general wrapper is ContentInfo. Its contentType field is an object identifier that names the type of content, and its optional content field carries the value defined for that type. If content is omitted, its value must be supplied by other means.

The RFC defines six content types: data, signed-data, enveloped-data, signed-and-enveloped-data, digested-data, and encrypted-data. Data contains an octet string without cryptographic enhancement. The enhanced types can contain another content type, so an outer structure can add protection to inner content. The ordering of fields supports single-pass processing in several types.
sections.plainLanguage: Each object identifies what kind of content it carries. A content type can wrap plain data or add a digest, signature, or encryption around other content.

sections.title: Signed Data and Verification
sections.content:
Signed-data contains content and an encrypted message digest for zero or more signers. To create it, a sender computes a digest for each signer, encrypts the digest and associated information with that signer's private key, and collects the result in a SignerInfo. Certificates and certificate-revocation lists may also be included.

A recipient uses the signer's public key to recover the digest and compares it with a digest computed independently from the content. The public key can be included in a certificate or identified through the certificate issuer and serial number. Optional authenticated attributes are covered by the signature; if present, they must include the content type and message digest. A signed-data object with no signers can carry certificates and revocation lists without a signature.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature lets a recipient check whether content matches a digest protected with the signer's private key. The recipient uses the public key to recover and compare that digest.

sections.title: Envelopes, Digests, and Encrypted Data
sections.content:
Enveloped-data encrypts content with a randomly generated content-encryption key. The sender encrypts that key separately for each recipient using the recipient's public key. Each recipient uses its private key to recover the content key and decrypt the message. At least one recipient is required.

Signed-and-enveloped-data combines encryption for recipients with signatures from one or more signers. Its signature digest is encrypted first with the signer's private key and then with the content key. Digested-data carries a message digest that a recipient can recompute to check content integrity. Encrypted-data carries encrypted content but no recipients or encrypted keys; key management happens by other means, such as a password for local storage.
sections.plainLanguage: An envelope encrypts content with a shared key, then encrypts that key separately for each recipient. Digested-data carries a check value, while encrypted-data assumes that keys are handled separately.

sections.title: Object Identifiers and Version 1.5 Changes
sections.content:
The RFC defines seven object identifiers: one for PKCS #7 and one for each of its six content types. The identifiers appear in the contentType field of ContentInfo.

Version 1.5 adds a certificate-revocation-list type, permits certificates and revocation lists to be distributed without signatures, revises signed-data and signed-and-enveloped-data, describes content-encryption padding, and adds encrypted-data. The Security Considerations section says that security issues are discussed throughout the memo. This RFC is an Informational publication of the RSA Laboratories specification, not an Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: Each of the six content types has its own identifier, so software can recognize how to process it. Version 1.5 added revocation-list support and a content type for encrypted data.
